entries.seminar_title: The Gravity of Wildfire Smoke: Avoidance Costs Revealed by Mobility Data
entries.speaker: Clara Berestycki
entries.abstract: This paper estimates the cost of wildfire smoke revealed by trip choices in Northern California in 2018. Using individual smartphone movement data and a discrete-choice model, I estimate the impact of wildfire smoke on activity participation and destination choice. Exploiting the extensive choice set observed in the smartphone data, I model trip flows as a gravity equation that includes smoke at the destination. People substitute away from smoky destinations and activities, and air quality alerts increase avoidance behavior. Outdoor trips are reduced the most, but trips to work and other destinations also decline with smoke. Based on estimated willingness to travel, these avoidance costs are about $500 million, adding 24% to the mortality burden of the same wildfire smoke season.

entries.seminar_title: The Optimality of Majority Rule: An Information-Choice Perspective
entries.speaker: Nina Bobkova
entries.abstract: How does the voting rule shape what a committee learns before voting? I study voters who choose between learning about a proposal’s common quality, and its consequences for themselves — their taste. Higher voting rules lead to less learning about quality and more about taste: being pivotal requires greater support from others, which provides favorable evidence about quality and makes quality learning relatively less valuable. A consensus paradox arises: requiring broader consensus can generate less of it. Supermajority rules are welfare dominated by an equilibrium under simple majority, and might always reject the proposal in large committees.

entries.seminar_title: Distributional Effects of Exclusive Dealing in Retail Real Estate
entries.speaker: Camilla Schneier
entries.abstract: I study the welfare implications of exclusive dealing in U.S. retail. Using a novel dataset, I document widespread use of contracts that restrict local entry by rival stores. Stores with exclusives face fewer competitors and higher prices, suggesting anticompetitive effects, yet many grocers in under-served neighborhoods use them, implying potential entry benefits in low-demand markets. I estimate a structural model of household store choice and a landlord–retailer entry game to capture equilibrium pricing and entry. Exclusive dealing benefits landlords and large retailers. A ban raises welfare for some households but increases the number of households living in food deserts.
